items.t: AI-assisted UI design: a workflow that keeps taste in the loop
items.d: Generators are fast but average. Split the job: humans set direction and constraints, AI explores variants, humans curate and polish.

items.t: Prompting for UI: write specs, not wishes
items.d: "Modern and clean" means nothing to a model. Name layout, tokens, states, content and what to avoid.

items.t: Design-to-code with AI: map to your components, not to pixels
items.d: Pixel-perfect export creates throwaway code. Give the agent your component registry and tokens via MCP so output reuses what you already ship.

items.t: Teaching agents taste: how design skills de-slop AI interfaces
items.d: Skills like frontend-design, taste-skill and impeccable package opinions as files agents load on demand. Here is how to combine them.

items.t: Component composition: why headless + copy-paste won
items.d: Radix behaviour, your styles, code you own. Compound components keep APIs small and make AI edits safer.

items.t: Motion that feels right: purpose, duration, easing, restraint
items.d: Most UI motion should be under 300ms, ease-out, and skipped for frequent actions. Spectacle belongs on marketing pages, not in tools.

items.t: Dark mode done right: tokens, elevation and contrast
items.d: Dark mode is a second palette, not an inverted one. Use semantic tokens, lighter surfaces for elevation, and desaturated accents.

items.t: Accessibility in AI-generated UI: the checks models skip
items.d: Generated UIs look fine and fail keyboards and screen readers. Start from accessible primitives, then audit against WCAG 2.2.

items.t: v0 in practice: from a prompt to shadcn code you can keep
items.d: v0 is strongest when you treat it as a shadcn/Tailwind code generator, not a design oracle. Brief it like an engineer, then pull the code into your repo.

items.t: Lovable and Bolt: when prompt-to-UI becomes prompt-to-app
items.d: Both tools build whole apps, so design quality now competes with data, auth and deploys for attention. How to keep the look from being an afterthought.

items.t: Aceternity UI deep dive: spectacle, used sparingly
items.d: Copy-paste React + Tailwind + Motion effects that made the "fancy" landing look popular. Which pieces carry a page and which turn it into a demo reel.

items.t: Magic UI deep dive: animated components that install like shadcn
items.d: An open-source (MIT) set of motion components distributed through the shadcn registry. Best picks for SaaS pages and how to keep them accessible.

items.t: Cult UI deep dive: tactile components with personality
items.d: shadcn-compatible components that feel physical: dynamic islands, textured buttons, expandable cards. How to borrow personality without breaking consistency.

items.t: shadcn blocks and registries: page sections as source code
items.d: Blocks (dashboards, sidebars, login pages) install with one CLI command, and any team can publish its own registry. Why this is the best substrate for AI agents.

items.t: Typography for AI-generated UI: the fastest way to look less generic
items.d: Generators default to one sans at three sizes. A type scale, a second typeface, tighter tracking on display sizes and real line lengths fix most of it.

items.t: OKLCH colour systems: palettes that survive dark mode
items.d: OKLCH keeps perceived lightness consistent across hues, so you can generate scales and dark themes by math instead of eyeballing. Tailwind v4 uses it by default.

items.t: Landing page teardown: what Linear and Vercel get right
items.d: Two widely copied developer-tool homepages, read as a list of decisions: one message, product as hero image, dark restraint, and proof placed right after the promise.

items.t: Dashboard patterns that hold up: from KPI strip to drill-down table
items.d: AI tools love to generate twelve charts. Good dashboards answer three questions in order: is it OK, what changed, why. A layout and a component list for each.

items.t: Design tokens for agents: the file that makes AI output on-brand
items.d: A machine-readable token file (the W3C DTCG format) plus a short usage note beats any adjective in a prompt. Structure, naming, and how to hand it to an agent.
